planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; brass buttons spreads by creeping rhizomes to knit into a solid carpet within a season or two under consistent moisture.

directions: Plant divisions or starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; brass buttons is a low, mat-forming New Zealand groundcover with finely divided, fern-like bronze-green foliage that spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a dense, textural carpet — a favorite substitute for turf in small shaded paths, between stepping stones, and as a soft, non-mowed filler around larger plants. Tiny, button-like yellow-green flowers appear in summer but are inconspicuous against the foliage, which is the main ornamental feature. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and stays low without mowing. Keep the soil from drying out for extended periods, since it thins in prolonged drought, and give it some afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage from scorching. Divide congested patches in spring to fill in bare spots or start new plantings elsewhere.

planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping speedwell roots as it spreads and fills in steadily over one to two seasons.

directions: Plant divisions or starter plugs in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping speedwell forms a dense, very low evergreen-to-semi-evergreen mat of tiny, glossy, rounded leaves studded in late spring with a profusion of small, pale blue to lilac flowers that briefly turn the whole mat into a haze of color. It roots as it spreads along the ground, tolerating light foot traffic, which makes it a popular filler between stepping stones and pavers and a low, tidy edging for shaded rock gardens. More heat and drought tolerant once established than moss-like alternatives such as Irish moss, though it still performs best with regular moisture and some relief from the most intense afternoon sun in hot climates. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat neat and encourage denser regrowth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Himalayan fleeceflower spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a dense mat and tolerates the dry shade found under mature trees once established.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Himalayan fleeceflower forms a dense, weed-suppressing mat of lance-shaped leaves topped from midsummer into fall with upright, bottlebrush-like spikes of small pink flowers that age gradually to a deep russet-red, so a single planting shows two-tone color as older and newer spikes bloom side by side. Foliage takes on attractive bronze-red tones in fall and persists semi-evergreen into winter in milder climates. It spreads at a steady, moderate pace by rhizomes, tolerates dry shade under trees better than many groundcovers once established, and needs little maintenance beyond cutting back old flower spikes and foliage in late winter before new growth begins. A dependable, long-blooming groundcover for the front of a shaded border or beneath open shrubs.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained to boggy soil in partial shade; sheep laurel grows naturally in acidic bogs, barrens, and open woodland margins across eastern North America and needs the same acidic, humus-rich conditions as its relative mountain laurel.

directions: Plant in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained to boggy soil in partial shade; sheep laurel is a low, compact native evergreen shrub of eastern bogs, barrens, and cutover woodland, closely related to mountain laurel but shorter and distinguished by its flowering habit — clusters of small, deep rose-pink, cup-shaped flowers appear along the stem below the current year's new leafy growth rather than at the branch tips, giving mature plants a distinctive layered look with new green growth rising above a band of bloom in early summer. It is a useful native shrub for the acidic, moist end of a woodland or bog garden and provides nectar for native bees and other pollinators. As the common names 'sheep laurel' and 'lambkill' warn, all parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins that are toxic if ingested by livestock and by people — keep it out of pastures and away from grazing animals, and do not consume any part of the plant. Prune lightly after flowering only if needed to shape; it resents heavy cutting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, consistently wet to constantly moist, peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; leatherleaf is a true bog plant native to northern peatlands and needs saturated, acidic conditions to thrive.

directions: Plant in acidic, consistently wet to constantly moist, peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; leatherleaf is a low, spreading, evergreen native shrub of northern bogs and peatlands, with small, leathery, scaly-textured, dull green leaves along arching stems that line up in tidy rows of small white bell-shaped flowers in early spring, often blooming while there is still ice at the bog's edge. It is one of the first shrubs to bloom in the northern wetland calendar and a valuable early nectar source for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Growing naturally in permanently saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat, it is a plant for a true bog garden or a rain garden basin engineered to stay consistently wet with acidic soil, not an ordinary moist border — it does not tolerate normal garden soil or drying out. Where conditions suit it, leatherleaf spreads slowly into low colonies and needs essentially no maintenance beyond leaving it undisturbed.
